draft.title: War Communism and the Red Terror
card: War Communism was the Bolsheviks' economic policy during the Civil War, from 1918 to 1921. Its aim was to feed the Red Army and the cities and to keep the Bolsheviks in power.
Grain requisitioning
Armed squads took grain from peasants, with little or no payment. Peasants had less reason to grow extra, so some planted less.
State control of industry
The state took over large factories and directed what they made. Private trade was banned, and workers were tightly controlled.
Red Terror
From 1918 the Bolsheviks used the Cheka, their secret police, to arrest, imprison and execute people seen as enemies of the revolution. The aim was to crush opposition through fear.
draft.remember: War Communism took grain and ran industry for the war effort, while terror silenced opponents. Together they brought hunger and revolt.

a.q: Why did grain requisitioning help cause famine in Russia?
opts: Peasants had less reason to grow extra grain, so output fell
Peasants were paid well, so they chose to stop farming
The Cheka banned peasants from owning any farm land at all
Factories stopped making goods, so cities bought less grain
a.why: Armed squads took grain with little or no payment, so some peasants planted less. Less grain meant hunger. Factory control also mattered under War Communism, but the card links the famine to the loss of any reason to grow extra grain.
a.clue: Think about what a peasant gained from growing more grain.

b.q: In 1921 peasants in a grain-growing region rose up against the Bolsheviks. Which policy most directly caused their anger?
opts: Armed squads taking their grain with little or no payment
The state taking over large factories in the cities
The Cheka arresting people seen as enemies of the revolution
The ban on private trade in city shops and markets
b.why: Peasants were the ones whose grain was taken, so requisitioning hit them most directly. The Red Terror and the factory takeover also caused hardship, but they did not strip peasants of their harvest.
b.clue: Which policy took something from farmers themselves?

a.best: Peasants had less reason to grow extra grain, so output fell

b.best: Armed squads taking their grain with little or no payment

problems.detail: The point is that War Communism caused famine and revolt, but the card never mentions either. It stops at 'some planted less', and only the remember line says 'hunger and revolt'. The card should state the famine of 1921 and peasant revolts such as Tambov, which question b relies on.
The why says 'the card links the famine to the loss of any reason to grow extra grain', but the card does not mention famine at all. The question asks students to make a link the card never teaches.

proposal.title: War Communism and the Red Terror
card: War Communism was the Bolsheviks' economic policy during the Civil War, from 1918 to 1921. The state took over large factories, banned private trade and took grain to feed the Red Army and the cities.
Grain requisitioning

Armed squads took grain from peasants with little or no payment, so peasants had less reason to grow extra and many planted less. Along with drought, this helped cause the famine of 1921 to 1922, in which millions died.
Red Terror
From 1918 the Cheka, the Bolshevik secret police, arrested, imprisoned and executed people seen as enemies of the revolution. The aim was to crush opposition through fear.
Revolt
Anger at grain requisitioning led to peasant revolts, such as the Tambov revolt of 1920 to 1921. In March 1921 sailors at the Kronstadt naval base also rebelled.
proposal.remember: Seizing grain and using terror kept the Bolsheviks going in the war, but by 1921 it had brought famine and revolt.

a.q: Why did grain requisitioning help cause famine in Russia?
opts: Peasants had less reason to grow extra grain, so output fell
Peasants were paid well, so they chose to stop farming
The Cheka banned peasants from owning any farm land at all
Factories stopped making goods, so cities bought less grain
a.why: Armed squads took grain with little or no payment, so many peasants planted less. With drought, the smaller harvests helped cause the famine of 1921 to 1922. The factory option is tempting, but the card links the famine to falling grain output, not to what factories made.
a.clue: Think about what a peasant gained from growing more grain.

b.q: In 1921 peasants in a grain-growing region rose up against the Bolsheviks. Which policy most directly caused their anger?
opts: Armed squads taking their grain with little or no payment
The state taking over large factories in the cities
The Cheka arresting people seen as enemies of the revolution
The ban on private trade in city shops and markets
b.why: Peasant revolts such as Tambov grew out of anger at grain requisitioning, which stripped peasants of their harvest. The Red Terror and the factory takeover also caused hardship, but they did not take grain from the peasants themselves.
b.clue: Which policy took something from farmers themselves?
